summaries.summary: RNNs, including LSTM, are standard for sequence modeling but cannot parallelize feature or state computation across very long sequences.
CNNs parallelize sequence encoding and scale to long sequences, but traditional pooling cannot fully use large-scale sequence order information.
QRNNs combine CNN-like parallelism with RNN-like sequence order dependence, outperforming strong LSTM baselines on three natural language tasks while reducing computation time.
Each QRNN layer has convolutional and pooling subcomponents, with parallelism across minibatches, sequence dimensions, and feature dimensions.
The QRNN convolutional subcomponent uses masked convolutions in the timestep dimension so each timestep cannot access future timesteps.
Additional convolutions with separate filter banks produce elementwise gate vectors, with candidate vectors using INLINEFORM0 and gates using an elementwise sigmoid.
INLINEFORM0, INLINEFORM1, and INLINEFORM2 are convolutional filter banks, and filter width 2 reduces the equations to LSTM-like DISPLAYFORM0.
Larger convolution filter widths compute higher INLINEFORM0-gram features at each timestep and are especially important for character-level tasks.
QRNN pooling functions use familiar LSTM elementwise gates, with dynamic average pooling as the simplest forget-gate-only option.
f-pooling, fo-pooling, and ifo-pooling initialize INLINEFORM0 or INLINEFORM1 to zero and require negligible computation time despite sequential recurrence.
A single QRNN layer performs input-dependent pooling and a gated linear combination, while two or more layers should be stacked for complex functions.
Several extensions to the stacked QRNN are introduced because many recurrent and convolutional model extensions apply directly to QRNNs.
A robust regularization scheme inspired by recent work in regularizing LSTMs is an important stacked QRNN extension.
Recurrent dropout schemes, including variational inference–based dropout BIBREF13 and zoneout BIBREF14, provide more powerful and less destructive LSTM regularization.
Variational inference–based dropout locks recurrent dropout masks across timesteps, while zoneout copies selected channels between timesteps without modification.
Because QRNNs lack recurrent weights, zoneout was extended by keeping previous pooling states for stochastic channels, equivalent to modifying INLINEFORM0 or applying dropout on INLINEFORM1.
The pooling function need not be modified, but off-the-shelf dropout rescaling should be removed, and ordinary dropout is also applied between layers.
Densely-connected QRNN layers use skip-connections between every layer, improving gradient flow and convergence but requiring quadratic parameter count.
Dense QRNN connections include input embeddings and every QRNN layer, concatenating each layer's input to its output and using only the last layer's output.
QRNN encoder–decoder models use a QRNN encoder and attention-enhanced modified QRNN decoder because feeding only the last encoder hidden state would limit decoder power.
Each decoder QRNN layer's convolution outputs are supplemented at every timestep with a linearly projected copy of the corresponding last encoder state.
Soft attention computes an attentional sum of encoder hidden states using dot products with decoder un-gated hidden states and INLINEFORM1 over encoder timesteps.
INLINEFORM0 is the last layer.
The attention procedure's first step is quadratic in sequence length but takes significantly less time than linear and convolutional layers.
QRNNs are evaluated on document-level sentiment classification, language modeling, and character-based neural machine translation, outperforming equal-hidden-size LSTM models while improving speed.
The IMDb movie review dataset has 25,000 positive and 25,000 negative reviews, equal train and test sets, and average document length of 231 words.
The best IMDb development performance used a four-layer densely-connected QRNN with 256 units per layer, 300-dimensional cased GloVe embeddings, dropout of 0.3, and RMSprop.
On IMDb, QRNN train time per epoch was 3.2x faster than cuDNN LSTM, with a 16x speed gain possible for specific batch sizes and sequence lengths.
Visualized final QRNN hidden states on an IMDb example show interpretable changes due to elementwise recurrent pooling and delayed channel interaction.
The language modeling experiment replicates BIBREF2 and BIBREF13 using a standard preprocessed version of the Penn Treebank (PTB) by BIBREF25.
A gated QRNN with 2 layers and 640 units used filter width INLINEFORM0 of two timesteps, with zoneout applied to the recurrent pooling layer.
PTB training used SGD without momentum, learning rate 1 for six epochs then decayed by 0.95 for 72 epochs, gradient norm rescaling above 10, and zoneout dropout ratio 0.1.
The gated QRNN with zoneout is highly competitive, and QRNN without zoneout strongly outperforms medium LSTMs without recurrent dropout.
Without zoneout, QRNN required early stopping, while small zoneout removed that need and achieved competitive perplexity to the variational LSTM of BIBREF13.
On PTB with an NVIDIA K40 GPU, QRNN was substantially faster than standard and cuDNN LSTMs, with softmax and optimization overhead becoming comparable bottlenecks.
cuDNN RNN primitives do not natively support recurrent dropout, so state-of-the-art regularized LSTMs at cuDNN-like speeds would likely require a custom kernel.
IWSLT German–English spoken-domain translation uses 209,772 sentence pairs, mean lengths of 103 German and 93 English characters, a 300-character cutoff, and 187 Unicode code points.
The best TED.tst2013 development performance used a four-layer encoder–decoder QRNN with 320 units per layer, 10 epochs, minibatches of 16 examples, Adam, and beam width 8.
The QRNN outperformed an equal-sized four-layer encoder–decoder LSTM with attention and dropout of 0.2, almost matching a word-level attentional baseline.
QRNNs relate to strongly-typed recurrent neural networks, including T-RNN, T-GRU, and T-LSTM, though some QRNN models with attention or skip-connections are not strongly typed.
Hybrid convolutional–recurrent models apply CNNs before LSTMs or GRUs for text classification and character-level machine translation, enabling parallelism and reduced sequence length.
The QRNN encoder–decoder shares parallelism and path-length properties with ByteNet BIBREF33, which targets parallelism, linear-time complexity, and short paths between words.
QRNNs exploit both parallelism and context, giving better predictive accuracy than equal-hidden-size LSTM-based models with fewer parameters and substantially faster running.
Extensions to CNNs and RNNs often apply directly to QRNNs, whose hidden states are more interpretable and may serve as building blocks for long-sequence tasks.
The modified log-probability ranking criterion used in beam search for translation experiments is DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is a length normalization parameter BIBREF34, INLINEFORM1 is the INLINEFORM2 th output character, and INLINEFORM3 is source sentence length plus five characters.
At INLINEFORM0, the criterion becomes beam search with probabilities normalized by length up to the target length.
The ranking criterion can be computed at intermediate beam-search timesteps, avoiding separate reranking of complete hypotheses.
